result: In Experiment 1 (with reliable spatial cues), strongly lateralized (Li) chicks showed a left-to-right bias in numerical spatialization, selecting the 4th left item preferentially in binocular tests, while weakly lateralized (Di) chicks showed no directional bias. Li-chicks also outperformed Di-chicks in accuracy. This demonstrates that brain lateralization is fundamental for developing left-to-right oriented spatial-numerical associations.
evaluation: All three reviewers affirm this core finding. The editor states the study 'demonstrates how a left-right bias in the relationship between numerical magnitude and space depends on brain lateralization' with 'compelling' evidence. Reviewer 1 confirms 'the authors are successful in revealing that the lateralized brain is advantageous in the number sense' and that 'the left-to-right numerical representation appeared when the distance between items gave a reliable spatial cue.' Reviewer 2 acknowledges this as 'the first study to show how a L-R bias in the relationship between numerical magnitude and space depends on brain lateralisation.' No reviewer challenges these findings.

result: In Experiment 2 (with unreliable spatial cues), the left-to-right bias disappeared in both Li and Di chicks during binocular testing, and Li-chicks did not outperform Di-chicks. This demonstrates that spatial information is essential for the expression of directional numerical spatialization.
evaluation: Reviewer 1 explicitly notes that 'the left-to-right numerical representation appeared when the distance between items gave a reliable spatial cue,' implicitly acknowledging that without reliable spatial cues (Experiment 2), the bias did not appear. The editor and other reviewers do not challenge these findings. The contrast between Experiments 1 and 2 is central to the study's logic and is accepted by reviewers.

result: In monocular tests of Experiment 1, Li-chicks succeeded in selecting the 4th item when using either the left eye (right hemisphere) or right eye (left hemisphere), while Di-chicks failed in both conditions. This demonstrates that light-induced lateralization enhances cognitive performance in both hemispheres and supports the right hemisphere's role in spatial-numerical integration.
evaluation: Reviewer 1 states 'Behavioral evidence is strong enough to support their arguments' and notes the importance of 'light-exposure induced lateralization' for the findings. The editor describes the evidence as 'compelling.' No reviewer questions the monocular test results or their interpretation regarding hemispheric contributions. The findings are treated as supporting evidence for the main conclusions.

result: In the left eye/right hemisphere monocular condition of Experiment 2 (unreliable spatial cues), both Li and Di chicks failed to select the 4th item, indicating that the right hemisphere cannot process ordinal information alone without spatial cues. This suggests ordinality is not lateralized to the right hemisphere.
evaluation: Reviewers do not challenge this finding. The pattern of results across monocular conditions in both experiments is accepted as part of the overall evidence. Reviewer 1's statement that 'Behavioral evidence is strong enough to support their arguments' encompasses these monocular findings. The interpretation about right hemisphere limitations is consistent with the reviewers' acceptance of the spatial-dependence of the effect.

result: In the right eye/left hemisphere monocular condition of Experiment 2, Li-chicks succeeded in selecting the 4th item even without reliable spatial cues, while Di-chicks failed. This suggests the left hemisphere is more specialized for processing ordinal information and that lateralization influences numerical cognition even without spatial information.
evaluation: This finding is not explicitly discussed by reviewers but is part of the overall behavioral evidence that Reviewer 1 describes as 'strong enough to support their arguments.' The contrast between left and right hemisphere performance in Experiment 2 supports the hemispheric specialization claims that all reviewers accept. No reviewer challenges the interpretation of left hemisphere involvement in ordinal processing.

result: The right hemisphere plays a key role in integrating spatial and numerical cues, being specialized for both spatial and numerical information processing. The integration of spatial and numerical processing within shared cortical regions is fundamental to numerical spatialization, with hemispheric specialization and environmental stimulation jointly contributing.
evaluation: The editor states the study 'demonstrates how a left-right bias in the relationship between numerical magnitude and space depends on brain lateralization.' Reviewer 1 notes the study reveals 'that the lateralized brain is advantageous in the number sense, in which numerosity is associated with spatial arrangements of items.' Reviewer 1 also states 'Specification of the responsible neural substrates in the presumed right hemisphere is expected in future research,' acknowledging the right hemisphere's role as established by the current findings. All reviewers accept the hemispheric specialization framework.

result: Higher levels of brain lateralization enhance cognitive performance generally and specifically boost numerical abilities. Li-chicks outperformed Di-chicks in the sagittal test and monocular conditions, demonstrating that prenatal light experience stimulates brain development and hemispheric specialization, which enhances performance in spatial/numerical tasks.
evaluation: Reviewer 1 explicitly states 'the authors are successful in revealing that the lateralized brain is advantageous in the number sense' and notes 'it remains largely speculative as to whether the lateralized brains have a cognitive gain or a sort of fitness advantage' but that 'In the present study...the authors are successful in revealing' this advantage. The editor describes the evidence as 'compelling.' The performance advantage of Li-chicks is central to the study's conclusions and is accepted by all reviewers.

result: Background claims about the Mental Number Line (MNL) in humans, including its traditional characterization as left-to-right and culturally rooted, and evidence showing inconsistency across paradigms and reading directions.
evaluation: Reviewer 2 extensively challenges the framing around the 'Mental Number Line' terminology and the characterization of human numerical spatialization. The reviewer states 'I would query the way the experiment was contextualised' and notes 'they seem to be asserting that humans have a left-to-right (L-R) MNL. This is highly contentious.' The reviewer points out that 'evidence remains inconsistent across paradigms' and cites studies showing no L-R bias in humans. The reviewer requests the paper 'should be shorn of its misleading contextualisation, including the term "Mental Number Line."' After revision, the reviewer notes 'The background and terminology in the text have been significantly altered and clarified: Spatial Numerical Association (SNA) instead of Mental Number Line (MNL),' indicating the authors addressed these concerns by reframing the claims.

result: Spatial-numerical associations (SNA) have been reported in newborns, infants, and nonhuman animals, suggesting neural/innate origins and challenging the predominant role of culture. Nervous systems across species are prewired for relating numbers to space, though numerical spatialization remains flexible and subject to modulation by experience.
evaluation: Reviewer 2 raises a conceptual challenge: 'their clever experiment shows that an experimental manipulation creates the bias. If it were innate and common to other species, the experimental manipulation shouldn't matter. There would always be a L-R bias.' This questions whether the findings truly demonstrate innateness versus developmental plasticity. However, after revision, Reviewer 2 acknowledges the authors 'make important arguments for the evolutionary advantage of the bias' and accepts the study should be published. The tension between innate predisposition and developmental modulation remains somewhat unresolved in the reviewers' comments, though the overall framework is accepted.

result: Various theoretical accounts link SNA to brain lateralization but previously lacked direct experimental evidence. The biological mechanisms and neural underpinnings of SNA were largely unknown, and no research had directly investigated the effect of hemispheric specialization on number spatialization through direct manipulation.
evaluation: Reviewer 2 acknowledges this as 'the first study to show how a L-R bias in the relationship between numerical magnitude and space depends on brain lateralisation' and praises the 'Novel methodology for investigating the innateness and neural basis of a L-R bias.' Reviewer 1 notes 'it remains largely speculative as to whether the lateralized brains have a cognitive gain' before this study. The novelty and importance of directly testing lateralization's role is affirmed by all reviewers.

result: The experimental manipulation: lateralization levels in domestic chicks can be manipulated by controlling light exposure during embryonic days 18-21. Light exposure leads to asymmetrical stimulation creating strongly lateralized (Li) chicks, while dark incubation prevents lateralization creating weakly lateralized (Di) chicks.
evaluation: Reviewer 1 explicitly notes 'Brain lateralization was manipulated by light exposure during the terminal phase of incubation' and states 'The light-exposure induced lateralization, though quite unique in avian species, together with the lack of intense inter-hemispheric direct connections...was critical for the successful analysis in this study.' All reviewers accept this manipulation as valid and well-established. No concerns are raised about the methodology for creating lateralized vs. non-lateralized groups.

result: Methodological details: 100 chicks were tested across two experiments using an ordinal task where chicks learned to select the 4th item in a sagittal array, then were tested with the array rotated 90° in various viewing conditions (binocular, monocular left, monocular right). Experiment 1 had reliable spatial cues; Experiment 2 had unreliable spatial cues.
evaluation: Reviewer 1 states 'Behavioral evidence is strong enough to support their arguments' and describes the methodology approvingly. Reviewer 2 praises the 'Novel methodology for investigating the innateness and neural basis of a L-R bias.' No reviewer raises methodological concerns about the experimental design, sample size, or procedures. The methods are treated as sound and appropriate for testing the hypotheses.

result: Theoretical models (right-hemisphere dominance, emotional valence, BAFT) all acknowledge hemispheric specialization's role in SNA but make different predictions. The right-hemisphere dominance model provides the most comprehensive and parsimonious explanation, accounting for behavior across multiple contexts including both ordinal and magnitude comparison tasks.
evaluation: Reviewers do not challenge the theoretical framework or the authors' evaluation of competing models. Reviewer 1 notes 'Specification of the responsible neural substrates in the presumed right hemisphere is expected in future research,' accepting the right hemisphere framework. The theoretical discussion is treated as appropriate contextualization rather than a primary empirical claim requiring validation. No reviewer disputes the authors' theoretical synthesis.

result: Speculative evolutionary and ecological interpretations: establishing a left-biased anchor point may have evolutionary advantages for environmental scanning and numerical processing; lateralization variability may represent adaptive bet-hedging; the left-to-right bias may have evolved from scanning behaviors and been assimilated into numerical cognition.
evaluation: Reviewer 2 initially states 'The authors also speculate, usefully, on why chicks and other species might have a L-R bias. I don't think the speculations are convincing, but at least if there is an evolutionary basis for the bias, it should at least be discussed.' After revision, Reviewer 2 notes 'the authors take on this challenge and make important arguments for the evolutionary advantage of the bias is (see lines 138ff, 375ff, 444ff), though this is likely still to be controversial.' This indicates the speculations are viewed as useful but not definitively established—they remain open questions rather than supported conclusions.
